props.title: Gagarine

sections.content: **Gagarine** (2020) masterfully blends social realism with cosmic dreams in Paris's suburban housing projects. Like **La Haine** (1995) before it, the film captures life in France's banlieues, but through a uniquely hopeful lens. Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh transform the real-life demolition of the Cité Gagarine housing complex into a poetic coming-of-age story, following 16-year-old Youri as he fights to save his home. The film's visual poetry recalls the magical realism of **Beasts of the Southern Wild** (2012), while its focus on architecture and community echoes **The Last Black Man in San Francisco** (2019).

sections.content: The space exploration theme in **Gagarine** connects beautifully to other films about dreamers transcending their circumstances. Like **The Florida Project** (2017), it captures childhood imagination flourishing in precarious conditions. The film's namesake, cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, visited the complex in 1963, and his spirit of exploration infuses the protagonist's DIY space station creation. The attention to architectural detail and community bonds recalls **Tower** (2016) and **Citizen Jane: Battle for the City** (2016), both examining how built environments shape human experience.

The film's magical realist elements create a striking contrast with traditional banlieue cinema. Unlike the gritty realism of **Rust and Bone** (2012) or **Dheepan** (2015), **Gagarine** employs ethereal cinematography and zero-gravity sequences to elevate its story beyond social commentary. This approach shares DNA with **The Science of Sleep** (2006) and **Amélie** (2001), other French films that use whimsy to process reality. SUBHEAD: Architecture as Character

sections.content: The Cité Gagarine itself becomes a vital character, similar to the apartment complex in **High-Rise** (2015) or the hotel in **The Grand Budapest Hotel** (2014). The filmmakers, who previously documented the real building's demolition, treat the architecture with reverence while acknowledging its decay. This architectural focus recalls **Columbus** (2017) and **Koyaanisqatsi** (1982), films that meditate on the relationship between humans and their built environment.
